analysis.one_liner: Makes paid conversion therapy a consumer fraud the FTC and states can prosecute.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 198 House supporters all Democrats, never left the Energy and Commerce Committee and received no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare it illegal for anyone to charge money for practices claiming to change a person's sexual orientation or gender identity, treating such practices as consumer fraud. The Federal Trade Commission, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general could all enforce the ban through civil actions, and advertising that claims conversion therapy works or is harmless would also be illegal. Counseling that supports someone through a gender transition, or that helps a client explore their identity without trying to change it, would remain legal.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBTQ people, especially young people, whom the bill protects from paid practices that professional mental-health bodies say are ineffective and linked to depression, self-harm, and suicide. Families would be spared paying for treatment that the bill's findings say defrauds them.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to provide conversion therapy in exchange for payment, closing the gap left by the patchwork of state laws that cover only licensed providers.
Treats paid conversion therapy as an unfair or deceptive practice under the Federal Trade Commission Act, letting the FTC impose penalties on practitioners.
Bans advertising that claims conversion therapy can change orientation or gender identity or that it is harmless, cutting off the marketing that brings in new clients.
Lets the Justice Department and state attorneys general sue violators, so enforcement does not depend on a single federal agency.
Expressly protects counseling that assists a gender transition or supports identity exploration, so the ban cannot be read to block legitimate therapy.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who earns money offering conversion therapy, including practitioners operating outside state licensing regimes, and providers of services or products integral to those practices, who would face FTC penalties and civil suits.

drawbacks.text: The bill's ban extends to any compensated person, not just licensed clinicians, raising the objection that it reaches religious counseling and speech that some argue is protected by the First Amendment; the text itself acknowledges a First Amendment carve-out only for products or services integral to the practice, a line courts could contest.

The findings lean on professional consensus that conversion therapy is ineffective and harmful, but opponents dispute using federal consumer-fraud law to settle what they view as a question of values and parental rights rather than deception.
Because enforcement runs through the FTC and civil suits, it does nothing about unpaid conversion practices by clergy or family members, which would remain lawful.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real but narrow: it targets only paid conversion therapy and leaves unpaid religious practices untouched, and its breadth beyond licensed providers would likely face a court challenge. Still, the cost falls on a small set of practitioners charging for a practice major medical associations have found ineffective and harmful, while the benefit goes to the vulnerable people those practices target.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its consumer protection subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Ted Lieu introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, with 74 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded in the bill's action history; its last recorded action is that June 25, 2021 subcommittee referral.
All 198 recorded supporters — the sponsor and 197 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor joined.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of paid conversion therapy, including unlicensed and faith-based practitioners in the roughly two dozen states without their own bans, keep operating free of any federal fraud liability. No one else gained from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 74 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 197 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it more than 40 percent of the chamber's support.

for.name: Mainstream professional mental-health associations
for.role: Medical and counseling bodies cited in the bill's findings
for.what_they_did: Their determinations that conversion therapy is ineffective and harmful form the factual basis for the bill's findings.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; no markup or hearing appears in its action history.

against.name: House Republican members
against.role: Potential floor opponents with no cosponsors on the bill
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan backing typically needed to move through committee.

against.name: Faith-based and religious counseling organizations
against.role: Providers of conversion practices outside state licensing systems
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal conversion-therapy bans as an intrusion on religious ministry and parental choice, arguing the First Amendment protects their speech and counseling.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 198 supporters was a Democrat; no Republican signed on, and with Democrats holding a narrow House majority the bill never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Conversion therapy providers, including unlicensed and faith-based practitioners
industries.note: These operators charge for practices that major medical associations have found ineffective and linked to depression and self-harm. The bill would expose any of them, including those beyond the reach of state licensing laws, to FTC penalties and civil suits.

Legitimate therapists lose no practice: the bill expressly protects counseling that assists a gender transition or supports identity exploration. They gain a federal backstop against a fringe competitor practice their professional bodies have condemned.
